title: Singeetam Srinivasa Rao, Director of 'Pushpaka Vimana', Dies at 94
excerpt: The genre-defying filmmaker behind Pushpaka Vimana, Aditya 369 and Mayuri died in Chennai on October 3, drawing tributes from Jr NTR, Kamal Haasan and Jagan Mohan Reddy.
body:
• Singeetam Srinivasa Rao, the veteran filmmaker behind Pushpaka Vimana and Aditya 369, died on October 3 at Kauvery Hospital in Chennai. He was 94 and had been under treatment for age-related ailments, according to family sources.
  • Across more than six decades, he directed around 60 films in Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, Malayalam and Hindi, winning two National Film Awards and the Film Federation of India's Life Achievement Award in 2011.
  • Tributes poured in from Jr NTR, Kamal Haasan, SS Rajamouli and former Andhra Pradesh chief minister YS Jagan Mohan Reddy, who called Rao "a true pioneer and pathbreaker."

Veteran filmmaker Singeetam Srinivasa Rao, whose genre-defying films reshaped what Indian cinema dared to attempt, died in Chennai on Saturday. He was 94. Family sources said he passed away at Kauvery Hospital on October 3 after a decline in health linked to age-related ailments.

The news prompted an outpouring of tributes from across the film industry and politics, mourning a director who spent six decades refusing to stay in one lane — moving from social dramas to silent black comedy to time-travel science fiction.

Tributes pour in

Former Andhra Pradesh chief minister and YSRCP chief YS Jagan Mohan Reddy remembered Rao on X, calling him a "true pioneer" of Indian cinema.

https://x.com/siddaramaiah/status/2106643506353807547

"Indian cinema has lost a true pioneer and pathbreaker, who continued making movies even at the age of 94. Singeetham Srinivasa Rao garu's unmatched creativity, from silent marvels to sci-fi epics, inspires generations."

— YS Jagan Mohan Reddy, former Andhra Pradesh chief minister

Actor Jr NTR described the news as deeply heartbreaking, writing on X that Rao was "a visionary who thought far ahead of his time and created films that continue to feel fresh and relevant even as generations change," citing Aditya 369, Pushpaka Vimanam and Mayuri.

Kamal Haasan, who headlined several of Rao's best-known films, posted a reflection on the director's lifelong energy.

"Dying young need not be a tragedy. It can be glorious. Singeetham Srinivasa Rao is a great example. I have admired him since I knew him. Now I aspire to live like he did."

— Kamal Haasan, actor

Filmmaker SS Rajamouli said Rao taught a generation of directors that imagination was the only true limit in cinema, while actor Mahesh Babu also shared his condolences, according to industry reports.

A career built on experimentation

Born on September 21, 1931, in Gudur, Andhra Pradesh, Rao studied physics at Presidency College in Chennai before entering cinema as an assistant to director K. V. Reddy, working on classics including the 1957 epic Mayabazar. He made his directorial debut in 1972 with the Telugu film Neethi Nijayithi.

What followed was one of the most unpredictable filmographies in Indian cinema: more than 60 films across comedy, science fiction, fantasy, social drama and children's cinema. His Tamil film Dikkatra Parvathi (1974) won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film in Tamil.

Mayuri (1985), based on the life of dancer Sudha Chandran, won a record 14 Nandi Awards. Two years later came Pushpaka Vimana, a black comedy starring Kamal Haasan made almost entirely without spoken dialogue — a formal gamble that paid off with the National Film Award for Best Popular Film.

His partnership with Haasan also produced Apoorva Sagodharargal (1989) and Michael Madana Kama Rajan (1990). In Telugu cinema, Aditya 369 (1991) took audiences into time travel at a moment when Indian science fiction barely existed. He also directed a string of successful Kannada films starring Rajkumar, including Haalu Jenu and Bhagyada Lakshmi Baramma.

Still directing at 94

Rao kept working deep into his nineties. His final directorial, the musical fantasy Sing Geetham — produced by Kalki 2898 AD director Nag Ashwin and built around an idea Rao had carried for nearly four decades — was completed in 2026, when Rao was 94.

In 2011, the Film Federation of India honoured him with its Life Achievement Award, adding to a shelf that included two National Film Awards, five Nandi Awards, three Karnataka State Film Awards and three Filmfare Awards South.

What his films mean for the diaspora

For Indian audiences abroad, Rao's films remain touchstones of ambition. Pushpaka Vimana, with no dialogue to translate, travelled beyond language barriers on visual storytelling alone — and his willingness to attempt science fiction and silent comedy decades before they were fashionable is still cited by younger filmmakers as proof that Indian cinema can take creative risks.

Tributes from across the industry continued through the weekend.
